inputs.need:
I am a midwife and the practice development lead on the labour and birth unit of a hospital with about 4,200 births a year. Induction of labour now accounts for 38 percent of our births, up from 29 percent four years ago. Inductions are booked by the antenatal clinic into a fixed number of daily slots, but the unit is often too busy to start them on the booked day, so women wait at home or on the antenatal ward, sometimes for more than a day, and midwives say the delays and the evening surges of women arriving for induction make the workload unsafe at times.

We want to understand how midwives, obstetricians and women experience the way inductions are scheduled and started, before anyone redesigns the booking system. I think this is a qualitative study with interviews and perhaps focus groups with staff, and interviews with women who have had a delayed induction. The unit manager wants practical recommendations, not just themes.

I need help with the research question, who to sample and how many, whether to include the booking clerks and the bed managers, how to talk to women who had a difficult experience without causing distress, how to analyse the material so the findings can inform the booking system, and what ethics approval we need. There is no budget apart from my protected time, and the interviews have to fit around shifts.
inputs.constraints: No budget apart from one day per week of protected time for the lead midwife until July 2027. Staff interviews must happen outside clinical shifts or in protected study time. No contact with women within six weeks of giving birth.

response.title: How induction of labour scheduling shapes workload and experience on a labour and birth unit
response.subtitle: Qualitative study with staff and women before booking redesign
response.statement: Induction of labour rose from 29 to 38 percent of births on a unit with about 4,200 births a year. Inductions are booked into six fixed daily slots, but the unit often cannot start them on the booked day, so women wait at home or on the antenatal ward and induction admissions arrive in evening surges that midwives describe as unsafe. Before the booking system is redesigned, the unit needs to understand how midwives, obstetricians, booking and bed management staff, and women experience scheduling and delayed starts, and what they think would work.
response.whoAffected: Women booked for induction and their birth partners, midwives and obstetricians on the labour and antenatal wards, antenatal clinic booking clerks and bed managers.
response.whatHurts: Waiting of more than a day, conflicting information and anxiety for women; unsafe peaks of workload and moral distress for staff.
response.currentPractice: Six fixed daily induction slots booked by the antenatal clinic without reference to expected labour ward capacity; start times decided on the day by the labour ward coordinator.
response.whyNow: Induction numbers keep rising, and the unit plans to redesign the booking system in 2027.
response.constraints: No budget apart from one day per week of protected time for the lead midwife until July 2027. Staff interviews must happen outside clinical shifts or in protected study time. No contact with women within six weeks of giving birth.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Women start induction close to the time they were given, know what is happening while they wait, and are cared for by midwives whose workload is safe.
response.summary: Problem framed as a qualitative study to inform redesign of induction booking.

records.title: Waiting to be induced: midwives' and women's accounts of delayed induction of labour in two maternity units
records.authors: Rasmussen-Achieng T, Obi-Fairweather L, Kaplan-Mensah R
records.venue: Journal of Midwifery Practice and Experience
records.abstract: We interviewed 24 midwives and 16 women who had experienced a delay of more than 12 hours between the booked and actual start of induction of labour in two maternity units. Midwives described a mismatch between fixed booking slots and a labour ward whose capacity changed from hour to hour, and evening surges when several women arrived at once. Several midwives described feeling unable to give safe care during these surges and distress at sending women home. Women described feeling forgotten, receiving conflicting information about when induction would start, and anxiety about the baby while waiting. Both groups suggested that booking should be linked to the unit's expected capacity and that women should receive one clear point of contact.

records.title: Induction of labour start delays and midwifery workload on a labour ward: an analysis of two years of unit data
records.abstract: We analysed 1,862 inductions of labour booked over two years on one labour ward. In total, 41 percent started more than 12 hours after the booked time. Delays were more common on days when more than 5 inductions were booked and on days with more than 20 births. On 23 percent of shifts that included an evening surge of induction admissions, the midwife-to-woman ratio in the delivery suite fell below one to two. Women whose induction was delayed more often had their labour augmented and more often reported dissatisfaction in the postnatal survey. The analysis relied on electronic timestamps, which were missing for 6 percent of inductions.

response.synthesis: Two retrieved records, appraised at abstract level, after the first search failed. A qualitative study in two units and two years of unit data describe the same mechanism: fixed booking slots meet fluctuating labour ward capacity, delays of more than 12 hours are common, evening surges strain staffing, and women feel forgotten while waiting. Neither study involved booking clerks or bed managers, and neither tested a redesigned booking system. The evidence is thin but consistent, and it supports a qualitative study that includes the people who run the booking process.
response.gradeRationale: Two single-setting studies, one qualitative and one observational, consistent in direction; limited by setting, recruitment through the units and missing timestamps.
response.summary: Two retrieved records appraised; three source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Delays arise where a fixed booking process meets a labour ward whose capacity changes by the hour; the retrieved records describe the mechanism and its human cost but not the view of the people who make bookings and allocate beds. Women's experience while waiting and midwives' experience of surges are two faces of the same scheduling problem. A study that samples across the booking chain can show where redesign would help.

response.title: How induction of labour scheduling shapes delay, workload and women's experience: an interpretive description study
response.abstract: Aim: to understand how staff across the booking chain and women experience the scheduling and starting of induction of labour, and where delay and unsafe workload arise. Design: qualitative interpretive description with interviews and focus groups. Setting: one labour and birth unit. Results will follow analysis.

response.methods: Purposive sampling of midwives, obstetricians, coordinators, booking clerks, bed managers and women with a delayed induction; semi-structured interviews and focus groups; reflexive thematic analysis mapped to booking steps with SEIPS.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present themes by booking step and the redesign recommendations.
response.discussion: The discussion will compare the findings with the retrieved qualitative and unit data studies and with the unchecked leads once they are retrieved.
response.limitations: One unit; insider researcher; retrospective accounts.
